evals.prompt: My Flutter app using AtCollection shares data with another atsign, but nothing syncs — SyncService stays inProgress and shared items never arrive. How do I debug this?
evals.expected_output: Treats a stuck-inProgress SyncService as a wedged sync and DIAGNOSES it rather than assuming a single cause. Explains the common cause is unscoped sync: with AtClientPreference.syncRegex unset, sync covers the atsign's ENTIRE keystore, so one unrelated/dangling key from another app or namespace can abort the whole round (e.g. 'key not found : <key> does not exist in keystore'). Recommends scoping syncRegex to the app's namespace. Notes the atServer always syncs a small set regardless of the regex (shared_key reserved keys, the encryption public key, and namespace-less public: keys), and that scoping still works because the sync regex is an unanchored substring match — so your own namespace's cached: copies match anyway; sharing and decryption are unaffected. Also frames that reads are local-only, writes sync in the background, and completion is observed via SyncProgressListener (not the deprecated sync(onDone:)).
expectations: Diagnoses a wedged sync rather than assuming a single cause
Identifies unscoped sync (syncRegex unset covers the entire keystore) as the common cause
Recommends scoping AtClientPreference.syncRegex to the app namespace
Notes the always-synced key set (shared_key reserved keys, encryption public key, namespace-less public: keys)

Fix: create the watch() stream once and hold it in State (a late final field or initState) and pass that held stream to StreamBuilder; never call watch() in build(). If the query has runtime inputs (e.g. a filter), recreate the held stream when those inputs change — in the setState that changes them — not on every build.

evals.prompt: Process A writes a coordination value with atClient.put() and process B (a different atsign) immediately reads it with get() but sees nothing. How do I make the write and the read hit the atServer directly instead of waiting for sync?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the WRITE as the problem: with the default AtClientPreference.remoteLocalPref = RemoteLocalPref.localOnly, put lands on the local secondary and reaches the atServer later via background sync. Fix: put with putRequestOptions: PutRequestOptions()..useRemoteAtServer = true. Notes B's read of another atsign's (non-cached:) key is already a remote lookup by definition; if a stale cached: copy interferes, GetRequestOptions()..bypassCache = true forces a fresh read from the owner's atServer (and GetRequestOptions()..useRemoteAtServer = true covers same-atsign read-your-write). May mention the client-wide alternative remoteLocalPref = RemoteLocalPref.remoteOnly. Notes remote ops cost a round-trip / fail offline and are for coordination or read-your-write cases — AtCollection data stays on the default synced path (collections take no per-operation options; they follow the client-wide preference).
expectations: Identifies the WRITE as the problem: default remoteLocalPref = localOnly routes put local with background sync
Shows put with PutRequestOptions()..useRemoteAtServer = true

evals.prompt: I send a notification to another atsign telling it to start a job. Sometimes the job never runs and I have no way of knowing whether the other side ever received the message. My send() call always completes without throwing. How do I find out whether the notification actually got there?
evals.expected_output: Explains that send()'s future completing means only that the notification was accepted for delivery, not that it arrived, and that the id send() returns is the handle for confirmation. Uses notificationService.getStatus(id), and polls it until delivered or a caller-chosen deadline rather than treating a single reading as final — because NotificationStatusEnum has only delivered and undelivered, so undelivered covers still-in-flight as well as failed. Notes getStatus also returns undelivered with atClientException set when the status query itself failed, and that the two must be distinguished. For a finer diagnosis reaches for fetch(id), whose AtNotification exposes the server's richer vocabulary (queued vs errored vs expired) — warning that status is a String carrying a 'NotificationStatus.' prefix rather than an enum, so an equality check against a bare 'delivered' never matches, and that an expired or unknown id returns a near-empty AtNotification whose value must not be read. Points out the confirmation deadline must sit inside send()'s expiration (15 minutes by default), since an expired notification reports the same way as one that failed, so expiration should be set deliberately when confirming. Notes both calls are remote round trips that fail offline. Does NOT claim awaiting send() confirms delivery, does NOT treat one undelivered as a definitive failure, and does NOT confuse this fetch with AtCollection's deprecated fetch(). May note that if a guaranteed reply is needed rather than a delivery receipt, AtRpc is the right tool.
expectations: States that send() completing means accepted for delivery, not arrival, and the returned id is the handle for confirmation

evals.prompt: I wrap every SDK call in try { ... } catch (e) { log(e.toString()); }. When something breaks in production the log just says one short line like "Exception: Failed to fetch data" and I have no idea what actually went wrong or where. I also can't tell which of these I should be catching at all versus letting crash. How should I be handling errors?
evals.expected_output: Identifies two separate problems. First, the log is thin because toString() returns only the innermost message, while AtException accumulates a chained trace that getTraceMessage() returns in full (rendered as the intent followed by each cause) — so the fix is logging e.getTraceMessage() instead of '$e' or e.toString(). Second, the blanket catch (e) is wrong because it swallows programming errors: ArgumentError and StateError signal misuse (namespace without a dot, create on an id that already exists, mutating an item you do not own) and should be fixed rather than caught, so the catch should be narrowed to on AtException, the root of what the protocol layer throws. Notes that CollectionOpException and TimeoutException from dart:async sit outside the AtException tree and will not be caught by on AtException — and that CollectionOpException matters most, because an AtCollection write fans out per recipient and those keys fail independently, so it carries a per-key breakdown (results / failures / firstFailure, each OpFailure exposing atKey, op and a reason that is usually the underlying AtException) and means the write was only partially applied. Recommends branching on e.exceptionScenario (and/or intent) rather than matching message text, and flags that both are nullable. May mention that the exception types need no extra dependency because at_client re-exports at_commons and does not export its own deprecated AtClientException/AtKeyException copies, what specific operations throw (put, get, notify), that AtPublicKeyChangeException is not retryable because the value can no longer be decrypted by anyone, or that AtExceptionManager converts KeyNotFoundException into AtKeyNotFoundException so a handler written for the former may never fire. Does NOT endorse keeping toString(), does NOT advise catching ArgumentError or StateError, and does NOT tell the developer to add at_commons as a direct dependency.
expectations: Identifies toString() as showing only the innermost message and directs to getTraceMessage() for the full chain
Narrows the blanket catch (e) to on AtException
Explains ArgumentError and StateError signal programming errors to fix rather than catch
Notes CollectionOpException and TimeoutException sit outside the AtException tree
Recommends branching on exceptionScenario rather than message text, and flags it as nullable
Does not endorse keeping toString() or advise catching ArgumentError/StateError

evals.prompt: My app writes an item and shares it, then a later step reads the data back, and sometimes the read doesn't see the write yet. I added a loop that keeps checking syncService.isSyncInProgress and only continues once it's false, but it still fails intermittently. What's the correct way to wait until sync has finished before continuing?
evals.expected_output: Explains that polling isSyncInProgress (or isInSync()) is a check-then-act race: both are point-in-time reads, so the answer can change between the check and the next line, and neither tells you when it becomes true. Directs the developer to await syncService.waitUntilCaughtUp(timeout: ...), noting it is an extension on SyncService so it works on any SyncService reference with no cast or opt-in, and that there is no need to call sync() first because it triggers an iteration itself. Stresses that timeout must be passed: it is nullable with no default, a SyncStatus.failure while waiting deliberately does not reject the future, so the timeout is the only bound and without one a stalled sync waits forever. Notes it throws TimeoutException from dart:async, which is not an AtException. Explains the snapshot semantics — it completes when localCommitId reaches the server commit id as it stood at the time of the call, so remote changes arriving afterwards do not extend the wait — and that completion also requires the local push queue to be drained (pendingPushCount), since commit-id equality alone would miss writes queued after the round started. May mention onProgress for progress UI (its exceptions are swallowed and logged), or contrast it with SyncProgressListener as the tool for observing sync over the life of the app. Does NOT recommend polling isSyncInProgress or isInSync, does NOT use the deprecated sync(onDone:) or setOnDone, and does NOT claim the wait covers remote changes made after the call.
expectations: Explains polling isSyncInProgress or isInSync() is a check-then-act race
Directs to await syncService.waitUntilCaughtUp(timeout: ...)
Stresses timeout must be passed: it has no default and a sync failure does not reject the future
Notes it throws TimeoutException, which is not an AtException
Explains the snapshot semantics — it completes at the server commit id as it stood at the call
Does not recommend polling isSyncInProgress or the deprecated sync(onDone:)

evals.prompt: I inherited a Dart service that uses the atsign SDK. It calls atClient.notify(...) to tell the other side about changes, atClient.startMonitor(...) to listen, and atClient.uploadFile(...) to send attachments. It all compiles and my IDE autocompletes everything. Is any of this a problem?
evals.expected_output: Says yes — every one of those is annotated @Deprecated on AtClient, and compiling plus autocompleting is not evidence otherwise. Maps notify (and notifyAll / notifyChange) and startMonitor onto NotificationService: send(...) to publish and subscribe(...) to receive, since the whole group predates NotificationService. For uploadFile, explains there is NO drop-in SDK replacement — it and downloadFile / reuploadFiles / shareFiles are annotated as moved to the app layer and are slated for removal — so the app must encrypt the file itself, upload the ciphertext to storage of its choosing, and share the URL plus the decryption key as a normal encrypted item, leaving the platform with no plaintext. May also flag the stream / sendStreamAck pair as carrying the same removal notice, that startCompactionJob / stopCompactionJob are inert because commit-log compaction went with the commit-log-free keystore, that the atChops getter and setter are deprecated in favour of building the client from its keyfile, or that NotificationParams.forText is no longer supported. Does NOT present any of these as merely stylistic or safe to keep, and does NOT invent an SDK-side replacement for the file-transfer methods.
expectations: Says notify, startMonitor and uploadFile are all @Deprecated despite compiling and autocompleting
Maps notify (and notifyAll/notifyChange) and startMonitor onto NotificationService send() and subscribe()
States there is no SDK replacement for uploadFile — the file methods moved to the app layer
Describes the app-layer approach: encrypt client-side, host the ciphertext, share the URL plus key as an encrypted item
Does not present these as stylistic, and does not invent an SDK file-transfer replacement

evals.prompt: I have two atsigns that need to send each other jobs — either side can start one, and both have to answer the other's. I set up an AtRpcClient on each so they could call each other, but as soon as a request arrives I get UnimplementedError. I also want a progress indicator while a long job runs. How should this be wired?
evals.expected_output: Explains the UnimplementedError is by design: AtRpcClient is one-way and its handleRequest throws, just as the adapter behind AtRpc.server throws from handleResponse — neither helper covers a peer that does both. Directs the developer to construct AtRpc directly with their own class implementing AtRpcCallbacks, passing callbacks: this, and notes isClient and isServer both default to true so one object serves and calls. Describes the interface as two methods, handleRequest(AtRpcReq, String fromAtSign) returning an AtRpcResp and handleResponse(AtRpcResp). For the progress indicator, explains that implementing the interface is what surfaces AtRpcRespType.ack — AtRpcClient.call() deliberately swallows ack, completing only on success and raising on nack or error — and warns that correlating responses back to requests becomes the caller's own job, since nothing is completing a future for them. May mention that sendRequest adds each recipient to allowList so replies are accepted, meaning a peer's allow list grows as it calls out and is not purely the inbound boundary configured, that with allowAll true checking fromAtSign in handleRequest is the application's responsibility, or that noports_core's NPA implements AtRpcCallbacks directly. Does NOT suggest running two AtRpcClients, and does NOT claim AtRpc.server alone can make outbound calls.
expectations: Explains the UnimplementedError is by design because AtRpcClient is one-way
Directs to constructing AtRpc directly with a class implementing AtRpcCallbacks, passing callbacks: this
Notes isClient and isServer both default to true so one object serves and calls
Describes the interface as handleRequest(AtRpcReq, String) and handleResponse(AtRpcResp)
Explains implementing the interface is what surfaces AtRpcRespType.ack, which call() swallows
Does not suggest running two AtRpcClients

evals.prompt: I'm using NoPorts to reach a machine at a customer site from my Dart app. I now need to restrict which atsigns are allowed to open a tunnel to that machine — right now anything with my daemon's address seems able to try. Where does that get configured?
evals.expected_output: Says this is NoPorts' own access control, configured on the device daemon rather than through anything in at_client — sharing, AtCollection permissions and enrollment namespaces do not govern it. Names the two mechanisms: a static allow list of client atsigns (--managers) and/or a --policy-manager atsign that is consulted per request, noting at least one must be supplied and that when both are given the policy manager decides for atsigns not on the list. May mention that if a static list is not enough the extension point is package:noports_core/npa.dart — implementing NPARequestHandler.doAuthCheck, which receives the daemon atsign, device name, device group and client atsign — and that NPAImpl runs it as an AtRpcCallbacks service, making a policy manager an ordinary AtRpc responder. Directs the developer to noports_core and the NoPorts documentation for the actual configuration. Does NOT invent a NoPorts API, flag names beyond these, or a code sample for wiring authorization, and does NOT claim at_client's sharing or enrollment controls who can open a tunnel.
expectations: Says NoPorts access control is configured on the device daemon, not through at_client
Names both --managers (static allow list) and --policy-manager, noting at least one is required
States the policy manager decides for atsigns not on the --managers list
Directs the developer to noports_core and the NoPorts documentation
Does not invent NoPorts APIs or flag names, and does not claim at_client sharing governs tunnel access

evals.prompt: I have a Dart daemon that picks up jobs sent to it as notifications and writes each one into a billing table. Every so often, after I redeploy it, a customer ends up charged twice for the same job. The team sending the jobs insists each one was sent once. What's going on, and what should I do about it?
evals.expected_output: Identifies that delivery to subscribers is at-least-once, not exactly-once, so a duplicate is expected behaviour rather than a sender bug or a defect to report. Explains the cause: the client saves its read watermark only after a notification has been handed to the handlers, so a stop landing between the two leaves the watermark behind a notification and the next connection delivers it again — deliberate, because the alternative is silently skipping one nobody saw. Connects the redeploy to that stop. Recommends making the handler tolerate running twice on the same notification: deduplicate on the notification id, or make the effect idempotent (an upsert or a state assignment rather than an insert or an increment), rather than trying to prevent the replay. Does NOT blame the sender, does NOT invent a setting, flag or delivery mode that would make delivery exactly-once, and does NOT suggest that awaiting send() or polling delivery status on the sending side would prevent the duplicate.
expectations: Identifies delivery to subscribers as at-least-once rather than exactly-once, so a duplicate is expected rather than a bug
Explains that the read watermark is saved after the handlers run, so a stop in between causes the next connection to deliver the notification again
Attributes the duplicate to the redeploy stopping the client, not to the sender sending twice
Recommends an idempotent handler — deduplicating on the notification id, or an upsert/assignment rather than an insert/increment
Does not invent a setting, flag or mode that would give exactly-once delivery

evals.prompt: Every time my Dart daemon shuts down, the logs fill with errors — sync failures, notification failures, a couple of stack traces. Nothing actually seems broken and the next start is clean. Is my shutdown wrong, or is this just noise I should filter out of the logs?
evals.expected_output: Says this is neither a broken shutdown nor noise to filter: the app is reporting a deliberate stop as a failure, and the fix is in how it catches and branches, not in the log configuration. Explains that work a stop cuts short — and any later call on that client — fails with StoppedException, which is deliberately NOT an AtException precisely so that a fallback or retry written for an ordinary failure does not treat an intentional shutdown as one, and that a blanket catch (e) therefore sweeps it up and logs it as an error. Tells the developer to catch StoppedException by name and end the work quietly, placing that clause before any broader catch, since a broader one placed first wins. Explains the sync case specifically: a stopping sync service sends progress listeners one final event with stopped set true and nothing after it, and that event is built with syncStatus of SyncStatus.failure and an exception reading that the service has been stopped, so a listener branching on syncStatus alone reports the shutdown as a failure — check stopped first. Explains the notification case: subscribe, subscribeFiltered and startListening throw StoppedException on a stopped service, and send/notify let it propagate rather than returning an undelivered result, so a stop is not a delivery failure and retrying it achieves nothing. May mention that the client's own background work reports a stop once at warning with no stack trace, so the severe lines and stack traces are coming from the app's own handlers. Does NOT advise suppressing or filtering the log lines by message text or log level, does NOT describe this as an SDK defect or something to report, and does NOT suggest on AtException will catch it.
expectations: Identifies StoppedException as what a stop raises, and that it is deliberately not an AtException so on AtException will not catch it
Tells the developer to catch StoppedException by name and end quietly, ahead of any broader catch clause
Explains a stopping sync service sends a final event with stopped set, which otherwise looks like a failure, so a listener must branch on stopped rather than syncStatus alone
States notification calls throw StoppedException rather than reporting undelivered, so a stop is not a delivery failure to retry
Treats the logging as a symptom of mis-catching rather than advising the logs be filtered or suppressed
Does not call this an SDK defect and does not claim on AtException catches it

evals.prompt: My Flutter app asks another atsign's device for some data and shows a spinner until the answer comes back. It works fine normally, but if that device happens to be offline the spinner never goes away — no error, no failure, the screen just sits there forever. What am I missing?
evals.expected_output: Identifies that the request/response call has no timeout of its own: it completes when a response arrives, and if no response ever arrives it waits indefinitely, so an offline or unresponsive peer produces exactly this hang. Distinguishes the two things that look like they should cover it but do not — the send-retry count and the request expiry bound getting the request *delivered*, not getting an answer back, so a request that arrives and is then ignored has consumed neither. States the fix is for the caller to bound the wait itself, wrapping the call in Future.timeout (or equivalent) and handling TimeoutException from dart:async, choosing the duration from how long the responder legitimately needs. May note that the only other way the wait ends is the caller's own client being stopped, which errors it with StoppedException, and that neither TimeoutException nor StoppedException is an AtException. Does NOT claim an existing SDK setting, retry count or expiry already bounds the wait, does NOT suggest the fix belongs on the responder side, and does NOT recommend polling or a manual request-id correlation scheme in place of the existing call.
expectations: States the request/response call has no built-in timeout and never completes when no response arrives
Distinguishes request-delivery retry/expiry from waiting for a response, and says the former does not bound the latter
Tells the developer to bound the call themselves with Future.timeout and handle TimeoutException
Notes the caller's client stopping is the only other way the wait ends, via StoppedException
Does not claim an existing SDK setting, retry count or expiry already prevents the hang
